title: Audio Editing Tricks
intro: Comping, crossfades, timing and pitch. This is where a good take becomes a great one, and where most of the invisible work in a professional record actually happens.

tips.t: Swipe across the take you want with the pointer
tips.d: Inside a take folder, simply drag across the part of a take you want to hear. Logic builds the comp automatically and crossfades the joins for you.

tips.t: Put take-switching on keys you choose
tips.d: The take-selection commands ship unassigned. Search “Take” in Key Commands and put the first few on keys — auditioning take 3 against take 7 becomes two keypresses.

tips.t: Save your comp as a new comp before changing it
tips.d: The take folder menu has “Duplicate Comp”. Do this before every significant change and you can always go back to the version that was working.

tips.t: Flatten only when you are certain
tips.d: Take Folder > Flatten turns the comp into regions. Flatten and Merge creates a single continuous file. Neither is reversible after the project is closed, so keep the folder as long as you can.

tips.t: Zoom in on the joins and check them
tips.d: Every comp point is a potential click. Zoom right in on each transition and confirm the crossfade sits in a gap, not on a consonant.

tips.t: Move a comp edit point without redoing the comp
tips.d: Drag the vertical divider between two take sections to slide the edit point earlier or later.

tips.t: Crossfade every edit point, without exception
tips.d: Set the Fade tool as your secondary tool and drag across any region edge, or type values into the Region inspector's Fade fields. Fades kill clicks, and every audio edit needs one.

tips.t: Set default fade lengths in the Region inspector
tips.d: Type a fade‑in and fade‑out value once, select all your regions, and apply it to everything at once.

tips.t: Curve the fade after you draw it
tips.d: Drag the middle of a drawn fade with the Fade tool to bend it, or edit the Curve value in the Region inspector. An S-curve on a vocal edit sounds far more natural than a straight line.

tips.t: Use “Remove Silence from Audio Region” for noisy tracks
tips.d: Control-click the audio region and choose Split > Remove Silence from Audio Region (⌃X). It strips everything below a threshold you set and leaves separate regions — great for a live kit or spoken word.

tips.t: Add a tiny fade to the start of every region as policy
tips.d: Even 3 ms removes the click from a non‑zero‑crossing start. Do it to everything and you never chase a mystery click again.

tips.t: Flex Time is one keystroke away
tips.d: Press ⌘F to show Flex, choose an algorithm in the track header, and drag transient markers to fix timing without cutting anything.

tips.t: Pick the right Flex algorithm or it will sound wrong
tips.d: Slicing for drums, Rhythmic for guitars and loops, Monophonic for single voices and bass, Polyphonic for chords and full mixes, Speed for tape‑style stretching.

tips.t: Add flex markers either side before you move one
tips.d: Placing anchor markers on the neighbouring transients stops your edit from stretching the whole bar.

tips.t: Quantise audio with Flex enabled
tips.d: With Flex on, the region's Quantize field in the inspector works on audio exactly like MIDI. Drums snap to the grid without a single cut.

tips.t: Use Flex Pitch to fix a single flat note
tips.d: Switch the track's Flex mode to Flex Pitch, then drag the note blob vertically. The gain, vibrato, pitch drift and formant handles are all on the same blob.

tips.t: Reset a bad Flex edit rather than undoing repeatedly
tips.d: Control-click the flexed region and choose Reset All Flex Edits. It clears the region's flex data and starts you fresh.

tips.t: Use the Audio File Editor for true destructive edits
tips.d: Double‑click a region and switch to the File tab. Silence, reverse, normalise and pencil‑edit at the sample level. Changes here affect the file itself.

tips.t: Normalise regions non‑destructively with Gain
tips.d: The Region inspector's Gain parameter changes playback level without touching the file. Always try this before normalising.

tips.t: Strip silence at the file level to reclaim disk space
tips.d: After comping, File > Project Management > Clean Up removes audio files the project no longer uses — whole files, not unused portions. Back up first; it is genuinely destructive.

tips.t: Reverse a region for a riser in two clicks
tips.d: Select the region, then Functions > Reverse in the Audio File Editor, or apply the Reverse setting in the region inspector for a non‑destructive version.

tips.t: Commit edits with Bounce Regions in Place
tips.d: Bounce Regions in Place (⌃B) renders your gain, fades and flex into a fresh file. Convert Regions to New Audio Files (⌥⌘F) is the lighter tool — it makes a new file but does not print those edits.
